title.narrative: SPVO – AFYA: Advancing Farmer & Youth Access to Healthcare

description.narrative: Masaka is one of Uganda’s principal Robusta coffee-growing regions and is home to a large population of smallholder coffee farmers. Many farming households face persistent challenges in accessing healthcare and securing a stable income. The scale of these needs extends well beyond the reach of existing initiatives.The AFYA project addresses this gap through a complementary, farmer-centred approach. Working through cooperatives and other existing farmer organisations, AFYA explores locally grounded financing models that can help farmers access healthcare without relying on long-term donor or buyer subsidies.A sustainable approach to healthcare financingThe AFYA project aims to strengthen Uganda’s Robusta coffee value chain by reducing the impact of ill-health, lost productivity and poverty on farming households.At the heart of the project is an innovative financing model that enables farmers to access healthcare and repay the costs over time, in line with their coffee harvest cycles. Different financing mechanisms will be tested, including agricultural fintech solutions, Savings and Credit Cooperative Organizations (SACCOs) and Village Savings and Loan Associations (VSLAs).The aim is to identify a practical and sustainable model that farmers can manage themselves and that can be embedded within existing cooperative, trading and digital systems. This could help make healthcare more affordable and accessible while strengthening farmers’ financial resilience.What the baseline study foundA baseline study conducted demonstrated a strong need for this approach. The findings show that poverty, health shocks and limited access to financial protection are closely interconnected with income insecurity, working conditions and risks to children’s education.Key findings include:- Large households: Coffee-farming households have an average of seven members. Approximately 55% of respondents were men and 45% women, with young people aged 18–35 accounting for around 10%.- Unstable incomes: Coffee is the main source of income for most target farmers, but earnings are seasonal and often insufficient to absorb unexpected expenses. Farmers commonly rely on borrowing, selling assets or pre-selling coffee to traders at lower prices to cope with financial pressure.- High levels of poverty: Around 79% of coffee-farming households experience multidimensional poverty.- Limited access to formal finance: Most farmers rely on VSLAs and cooperatives to access financial services.- Frequent health shocks: 66% of households reported that at least one member had been ill during the three months preceding the study. Common illnesses included malaria, flu, ulcers and chronic conditions.- Delayed healthcare: Of the households that experienced illness, 47% delayed seeking healthcare, mainly because they did not have enough money available when care was needed.- Loss of income and education: Health-related shocks resulted in an estimated 11 lost working days per household and five missed school days per child over a three-month period.- Debt linked to healthcare:34% of households went into debt to pay for healthcare, while 24% pre-sold coffee to traders at low prices. These coping strategies can reinforce cycles of debt and income insecurity.- Risks to children: Financial and health-related pressures can increase the risk of children missing school or becoming involved in farm work, particularly during periods of peak labour demand. Some children were reported to participate in activities such as harvesting and carrying loads.- Vulnerable working conditions: Coffee production is largely carried out with limited mechanisation. Farmers face occupational risks, including exposure to agrochemicals, while the use of protective equipment remains limited.From assessment to actionBased on these findings, Phase B will focus on developing community-led, flexible and inclusive healthcare financing mechanisms, through existing farmer institutions.By addressing health shocks as an important driver of economic and social vulnerability, the project aims to improve access to healthcare, reduce financial stress, protect children’s education and strengthen the resilience of coffee-farming households in Greater Masaka.The success of the approach will depend on keeping the financing mechanisms simple, transparent and trusted by farmers, while ensuring that vulnerable households are not excluded.Building a model for wider useIf successful, AFYA could provide a scalable model for improving healthcare access within coffee-growing communities. The approach could be extended across Ndugu’s wider network and adapted by other sector partners.Shared financing structures could help reduce costs and make the model more accessible. The lessons from AFYA could also inform future programming and contribute to wider strategies for responsible coffee sourcing, farmer resilience and access to healthcare.Key lessons and results will be shared through relevant sector platforms to support learning and encourage wider adoption of effective approaches to healthcare financing and farmer resilience.
